title: Regional failover, degradation SLAs and hosting model intake with EmberTech
summary: Discovery focused on how Redwood's hosted/dedicated/private options support EmberTech's stringent latency SLOs and multi-region failover. Key concerns: graceful degradation strategies, cache warming after failover, SLA credits, and security/compliance for private deployments. Redwood AE/SE outlined regional routing, model variant fallbacks, and canary rollouts. Next steps: share security pack, run a short perf benchmark, and propose pilot scope.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes
Attendees: Sophia Chen (Redwood AE), Mateo Ruiz (Redwood SE), Jai Kaur (Redwood SE), Alicia Monroe (EmberTech Head of Infra), Daniel Park (CTO), Ravi Shah (Platform Lead), Lina Gomez (Security)

Auto-generated summary: EmberTech is evaluating options for hosting their LLM inference: hosted for speed, dedicated for predictability, private for compliance. They require 99.95% uptime with p95 latency under 200ms for interactive routes. Concern about degraded modes and regional failover.

[00:00] Sophia Chen: Hey everyone, thank you for carving time, um, I'm Sophia from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, with me is Mateo, our SE, and Jai who will cover some of the deeper routing stuff.
[00:12] Alicia Monroe: Thanks, Sophia, yeah appreciate it. I'm Alicia, head of infra at EmberTech. We — quick background — we run most customer facing inference in AWS EC2/GPU nodes behind an API gateway, and we currently have a homegrown autoscaler. We're exploring replacing that with Redwood for either hosted or dedicated, maybe private in the long run.
[00:35] Daniel Park: Hi all, CTO here, my main questions are around what happens during region-level outages and whether we can guarantee SLOs or at least degrade gracefully without breaking user flows.
[00:48] Mateo Ruiz: Great, thanks. To frame the convo, can you share the specific SLOs you need and which routes are most latency sensitive?
[00:55] Ravi Shah: Our target is 99.95% availability across API endpoints, p95 < 200ms for the chat autocomplete route, p99 is tolerated to be higher. We also have a batch embedding job that can be async. Critical flows are login-affecting and our chat UI.
[01:12] Lina Gomez: From security side, we need KMS integration, customer-managed keys for private deployment, audit logs retained for 1 year and SSO via SAML. SOC2 reports are also a gating item.
[01:26] Sophia Chen: Understood. High level: for Hosted we run multi-region control plane and route requests in-region by default but can failover to another region per policy; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools — predictable throughput — and Private runs in your VPC with a customer-managed control plane. We do support KMS and long-term audit log retention for Private.
[01:47] Alicia Monroe: When you say failover, how graceful is that? For example, if a region has a partial outage and we route to a different region, won't the model cold start and spike latency wildly? That's our core worry.
[02:01] Mateo Ruiz: Yes, cold starts are an issue. We have strategies: 1) prefix/KV caching (we call it prefix cache) which reduces rehydration cost, 2) warm standby model replicas in the target region kept at low utilization, or 3) sending traffic to smaller, lower-cost model variants as a degraded mode. Each has tradeoffs — cost, state consistency, and response fidelity.
[02:27] Daniel Park: Can you elaborate on the 'smaller model variant' idea? How do you maintain output quality expectations?
[02:33] Jai Kaur: Sure. We support model variant mapping in routing policies. For critical low-latency routes you can pin Model-A full to region, and have Model-A-quant or Model-B-compact as fallback. We recommend evaluating fallbacks with a set of prompts — Redwood Optimize can run regression tests pre-cutover, and we can block rollout if quality drops beyond thresholds.
[02:58] Ravi Shah: So during failover we could switch to a quantized variant to keep p95 under 300ms, accept some accuracy tradeoff, but maintain availability. Who actually orchestrates that switch — us or Redwood?
[03:12] Mateo Ruiz: You can define the policy in the console or via API. We also provide automatic fallback profiles that trigger by region health, latency thresholds, or error rates. It can be fully automated or require manual approval on first execution.
[03:29] Alicia Monroe: About caching — how do you handle KV cache consistency? Our workloads depend on some user-specific context, we can't have stale KV entries.
[03:40] Mateo Ruiz: Right, there's a distinction. Prefix/KV caching is best for shared system prompts or common context. For per-user KV we recommend encrypted, sticky session routing so sessions are routed to replicas with the right KV. In cross-region failover we can rehydrate KV from an async replication feed, but there will be a window of eventual consistency — depends on your tolerance.
[04:02] Lina Gomez: That eventual consistency window is critical. We need to quantify it for compliance — if an audit asks about data residency or log access, we must show the replication timeline.
[04:12] Sophia Chen: We can surface replication delay metrics in the console and in audit logs. For Private deployments we can also configure synchronous replication if you want zero window, but that increases latency and cost.
[04:26] Daniel Park: What's the SLA language around failover? If Redwood routes to a different region and we hit 2 minutes of elevated latency during rehydration, will that count against the uptime SLA or are there exceptions?
[04:38] Sophia Chen: Our standard SLA covers endpoint availability in a region; we do have exception language for catastrophic third-party outages. For cross-region failover that is triggered by our routing policies, we aim to keep the service within the SLA by using warm standby or model fallbacks. We can add explicit SLOs for degradation windows in an enterprise contract — e.g., credit for extended failover time beyond X minutes.
[04:59] Ravi Shah: Ok, how do you measure availability? Is it per-route? Per-token?
[05:05] Mateo Ruiz: Availability is measured at the route level (per API route/model combination) — we provide token-level latency histograms, error rates, and route-level uptime metrics. The console gives you p50/p95/p99 and a breakdown by region and model variant.
[05:20] Alicia Monroe: Let's talk about private deployment — we have strict data residency rules for certain clients. If we go Private, can we still use Redwood's model catalog or do we need to bring our own model artifacts?
[05:32] Jai Kaur: Private supports either: you can pull Redwood-verified open models into your private repo, or bring your own model files. For some compliance-sensitive customers we ship a private image and you keep control of keys and artifact storage.
[05:45] Lina Gomez: On KMS — can you integrate with our HSM-backed keys? We have an external HSM provider.
[05:51] Sophia Chen: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM via standard integrations. We'll need to run an architecture review to map endpoints and key usage. That would be part of the pilot scope.
[06:04] Daniel Park: Pricing tradeoffs are important. Dedicated sounds ideal for predictability, but cost will be higher. How do you help customers reason about latency vs cost?
[06:15] Mateo Ruiz: Redwood Optimize gives cost/perf profiles and suggests quantization levels and batching strategies. For interactive low-latency routes you might disable heavy batching and run smaller batch sizes at higher cost. We can model cost impact of keeping warm standby replicas too.
[06:31] Alicia Monroe: Does Redwood offer burst capacity? We have traffic spikes from feature launches.
[06:36] Sophia Chen: Yes, Dedicated includes optional burst capacity and autoscaling policies. Hosted offers burst across shared pools but with throttling/quotas. We can build guaranteed burst for enterprise contracts.
[06:48] Ravi Shah: On routing — is there an out-of-the-box multi-region DNS or do you recommend client-side routing?
[06:55] Mateo Ruiz: We do smart routing in the control plane. Typically DNS is regional but we attach a latency-based edge that selects nearest healthy region; traffic flows through our edge to the chosen region. For Private you can run similar logic inside your VPC with our routing agent.
[07:10] Daniel Park: Can the routing policy do weighted canary across regions? We want to test a new fallback in 5% of traffic first.
[07:17] Jai Kaur: Absolutely — routing policies support percentage-based rollouts, canary rules, and can automatically revert if error rates spike. You can combine this with quality gates powered by Redwood Optimize.
[07:29] Alicia Monroe: Any limitations around model sizes in private vs hosted? We have models at 70B and some at 13B.
[07:36] Mateo Ruiz: We support up to large model sizes in both, but in Private there may be infra footprint differences; we'll size GPU pools accordingly. For 70B we'd recommend multi-GPU instances and likely Dedicated or Private for predictability.
[07:51] Ravi Shah: Could you run us through a hypothetical incident flow? Say region A goes down at 2am — what are the steps and signal timelines?
[07:59] Sophia Chen: Briefly: 1) monitoring detects elevated error rates and increased latency, 2) routing policy activates failover — either automated or manual, 3) traffic shifts to standby region or fallback variant, 4) metrics show rehydration/cold-start latency spike — we emit an incident timeline and alert the customer. Typical automated failover aims to complete within 1-3 minutes if warm standby is enabled; cold starts may take longer.
[08:26] Daniel Park: That 1-3 minute window is important. Can we instrument synthetic p95 checks across regions to validate readiness?
[08:33] Mateo Ruiz: Yes, Redwood supports synthetic canaries and health checks per region; we can add probes that exercise specific routes and model variants and fail the routing policy open only when checks pass.
[08:44] Alicia Monroe: What about client-side retries? If our clients retry aggressively, we could double traffic during failover.
[08:50] Jai Kaur: We recommend retry-backoff with jitter and provide headers to indicate failover state so clients can make smarter decisions. Also, our gateway can surface 429 vs 503 to indicate degraded mode.
[09:01] Lina Gomez: For audits we need immutable incident logs. Does Redwood provide tamper-proof logs or do we need to ship to our SIEM?
[09:09] Sophia Chen: We provide signed audit logs and can stream logs to your SIEM or S3 bucket. Private deploy allows you to keep logs entirely in your environment.
[09:20] Ravi Shah: For the pilot, we want to do a short perf test: spin up a dedicated pool equivalent to our 95th percentile load, run synthetic traffic, and then trigger a region failover to measure latency delta. Is that feasible?
[09:31] Mateo Ruiz: Yes, that's a common pilot. We'll scope compute shapes, model variants, and traffic profile. We'll run two failover scenarios: warm standby and cold start, and measure p95/p99 and token cost.
[09:45] Daniel Park: Who needs to sign off internally? I want to loop Legal and Procurement early on if pricing looks good.
[09:51] Alicia Monroe: My team will evaluate infra fit; Lina will sign off security; Daniel will take executive sign-off. Procurement will step in for contract language and SLA negotiations.
[10:03] Sophia Chen: Good call. We'll include pricing scenarios for Hosted, Dedicated (monthly commit), and Private in the follow-up. We'll also surface expected unit cost per token for the baseline and degraded modes.
[10:15] Ravi Shah: One more question on rollback — if a fallback variant degrades quality significantly, can the routing policy auto-roll back to previous region even if it's unhealthy?
[10:25] Jai Kaur: We allow multi-conditional policies. For example, revert if quality gate fails AND error rates remain low in the original region. Typically you'd want to avoid routing back to a truly unhealthy region; policies can be tuned.
[10:38] Alicia Monroe: Any hard limits on how many concurrent fallback variants we can define?
[10:43] Mateo Ruiz: No hard limits — but complexity grows. We recommend a small set of tested fallbacks per route for manageability.
[10:51] Daniel Park: Let's talk about telemetry retention. We need 13 months of detailed telemetry for compliance.
[10:58] Sophia Chen: Enterprise packages support extended retention. For Private we can retain as long as you like within your storage. Hosted default is 90 days unless extended.
[11:09] Lina Gomez: On SSO, we need SCIM user provisioning and role-based access for developers vs ops. Does Redwood support that?
[11:16] Sophia Chen: Yes — SAML single sign-on, SCIM provisioning, and granular RBAC are supported. We'll share docs.
[11:22] Ravi Shah: Ok, I think we have enough to scope the pilot. Can you summarize the pilot deliverables?
[11:28] Mateo Ruiz: Pilot scope: 1) Dedicated test pool sized to 95th percentile, 2) two model variants (primary + quant fallback), 3) synthetic traffic replay, 4) failover tests (warm standby vs cold start), 5) telemetry capture and incident timeline export.
[11:44] Daniel Park: Timeline?
[11:46] Sophia Chen: If EmberTech provides traffic profile and credentials, we can kick off the pilot infra provisioning within 2 weeks and run tests over a 1-week window. So start earliest 2026-10-19 and finish by 2026-10-26.
[11:58] Alicia Monroe: Sounds reasonable. Any legal/data transfer concerns for Hosted? Some customers require that data never leaves EU.
[12:06] Sophia Chen: Hosted can be region-limited but not fully private; for strict residency we recommend Private with a local region deployment.
[12:15] Lina Gomez: Please send your SOC2, pen test summary, and a short architecture sketch of Private deployment.
[12:20] Sophia Chen: Will do. We'll attach them to the follow-up email.
[12:24] Ravi Shah: Alright, appreciate the clarity.

Recap (auto):
- Key asks from EmberTech: p95 <200ms, 99.95% availability, KMS/HSM, 1 year logs, SAML+SCIM, data residency controls.
- Redwood to deliver: security pack (SOC2, pen test), pilot plan, perf spreadsheet and estimated costs for warm standby vs cold start, and proposed routing policies for model fallbacks.

[12:54] Sophia Chen: Thanks everyone we'll follow up with the docs and the pilot plan. Any final quick Qs?
[12:58] Daniel Park: None from me. Thanks all.
[13:01] Alicia Monroe: Thanks, appreciate it.

End of transcript.
